title: History, closed
hook: the tradition has been broken and has healed, many times

segments.voice: Yesterday, carved blocks made again and ordination invited back from Siam. Your line: it renews. Did you take the first small step? Today closes this stretch of history. Day one thousand fifty-two.

Why spend so many days on hard history in a daily practice? That was the question this block began with, and the answer then was simple: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure. Since then you've heard about kings and monks, closed monasteries, wars, exile, killing years, empty niches in a cliff, and broken trust. You've also heard about rebuilding, apology, dignity, chaplains and temples far from home. Today we close the history, and hold all of it at once.
screen: `MADE OF PEOPLE.` → `FAILING AND ENDURING.` → `HOLD ALL OF IT AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of what we've walked through. First, the breaks from outside. Rulers protected the sangha and used it. Monasteries were closed by governments. Communities were scattered into exile, or nearly destroyed. Second, the harms from inside. Some Buddhist institutions backed wars. Some monks spoke for hate, while others spoke against it. Some teachers abused the trust placed in them. This block didn't pretend the tradition only ever suffered things; sometimes its own people did the harm. Third, the healing. Monasteries rebuilt in India with their old names. A sangha in Cambodia raised again from very few. Doors in China and Mongolia opened again. Apologies made. Dignity claimed in India by people once called untouchable. Ordination invited back across the sea. And fourth, the reason none of this surprises the tradition itself: anicca, impermanence. Everything made comes apart, including institutions. The teaching doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. What it offers is a way to stand while things come apart. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in a picture: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm." History has been a flood more than once. Again and again, people have built islands in it: a practice kept, a text carried, a door opened. Broken, and healed, and broken again. That's the history this path has been telling.
screen: `THE BREAKS FROM OUTSIDE.` · `THE HARMS FROM INSIDE.` · `THE HEALING, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `AN ISLAND WHICH NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: sit with gratitude. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind the people who carried this tradition through the hard years. Monks walking over mountains. A nun hiding a text. A grandmother in Phnom Penh who still remembered the chants. Carvers bent over wooden blocks. You don't need names. With each breath, let a little thanks go toward them. If your mind drifts to the harms, let them be there too. Gratitude doesn't erase them. It just stands next to them. The bell holds the time.
History. The long story of a tradition broken from outside and from within, and healed, many times, by people who rebuilt, carried and opened doors again. Today's word.
Your line: broken and healed. Tomorrow the festival year begins again. Today, thank one person, living or remembered, who helped put something in your life back together. Day one thousand fifty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember hard histories in memorial services, rebuilt temples and teachings on impermanence, and some dedicate merit or loving-kindness to those who carried the tradition through loss.

myth: this block told only harms done to Buddhists by others
it also told harms from inside: institutions that backed wars, monks who spoke for hate, teachers who broke trust.
the teaching expects institutions to come apart too
anicca, impermanence, applies to everything made, including temples and lines of teachers.
gratitude for those who carried the tradition erases the harms
the practice lets gratitude stand next to the harms, not over them.

fork.setup: the flood of history has swept through your monastery. what does the Dhammapada say the wise do?
options: wait for the flood to pass and do nothing
make an island by earnestness, restraint and control
leave the practice for something safer
fork.reveal: Dhammapada 25: the wise, by rousing themselves, make an island which no flood can overwhelm.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. everything made comes apart, institutions too: the reason breaking and healing are no surprise.

trapdoor: what you thought: history is the boring part between the teachings.
what it means: a tradition broken from outside and within, and healed, many times, by people.
what a scholar hears: anicca applied to the sangha itself, and Dhammapada 25's island amid the flood.

notes: Dhammapada 25 is quoted in Max Müller's wording from memory; please verify exactly.
The recap compresses days 1031–1051; every item was told in earlier days of this block with its own notes. Confirm the phrasing 'people once called untouchable' for the Ambedkarite day.
The practice's figures (a nun hiding a text, a grandmother in Phnom Penh who remembered the chants) are illustrative images, not sourced individuals; confirm acceptable or make more general.
Block H ends here; the carry points to the festival year (Block I) beginning tomorrow.

Editor pass: 'weeks' (an uncited count) changed to 'so many days'; 'has never asked' (an absolute claim) softened; 'many dedicate merit' softened to 'some'; the stock line 'not once, but over and over' replaced.

Audit pass: the teach filed wars and hate speech under 'breaks' from outside and listed 'debates still unsettled' (the women's ordination day) as a harm, which framed one side of a live debate as harm; regrouped so outside breaks and inside harms are distinct and the ordination debate is not called a harm; the myth reveal no longer calls rulers' use of the sangha an inside harm.
